strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and well-motivated limitation of existing NeRF-weight-processing methods: prior work such as nf2vec and Cardace et al. can only ingest a single predefined NeRF architecture.
It presents the first architecture-agnostic framework for processing NeRF weights by combining a Graph Meta-Network encoder with parameter-graph representations of MLP-based and tri-planar NeRFs.

The contrastive SigLIP loss is sensibly introduced to align embeddings of different architectures representing the same underlying object, and the t-SNE analysis provides useful qualitative insight into the effect of rendering versus contrastive objectives.

The experimental evaluation covers classification and retrieval, including cross-architecture classifier transfer and several unseen architectural variants, which supports the main claims to a reasonable degree.
In the single-architecture setting, the method outperforms or is competitive with nf2vec and Cardace et al. on their respective architectures.
The paper is generally clear, with good related-work coverage and sufficient implementation details in the appendix for a reader to understand the encoder, decoder, losses, and training setup.
Qualitative retrieval examples suggest that the learned embeddings capture object shape and color and exhibit some architecture invariance.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is incremental: the method largely combines an existing Graph Meta-Network encoder, the nf2vec decoder, and a standard SigLIP contrastive loss, without introducing a fundamentally new meta-network or graph-conversion technique.

The experimental validation is narrow: all experiments are on synthetic ShapeNetRender object-centric NeRFs, and only two non-state-of-the-art architecture families are considered (MLP and tri-plane). Hash grids, voxel fields, and real-world scenes are not evaluated.

The claims about arbitrary or unseen NeRF architectures are overstated. The unseen evaluations are mainly hyperparameter variants of the two seen architecture families; entirely new architecture types are not shown to be handled.

There are no multi-architecture baselines because no prior method can operate in that setting, but the single-architecture gains over nf2vec and Cardace et al. are small, and no rendering-plus-image baseline is compared despite being the natural naïve alternative.

The combined L_R+C objective is not consistently best: L_R is better for multi-architecture classification, while L_C is better for retrieval, which complicates the central claim that the combined loss is the preferred training objective.
Robustness is limited in several reported cases, e.g. very low accuracy for L_R on TRI-16W and for L_C on TRI-8C, and near-random cross-type transfer in the single-architecture setting.
There are no error bars or multiple-seed results, and the training cost is very high (~2 weeks on a single RTX 3090), raising reproducibility and practicality concerns.
The contrastive training setup requires paired same-object NeRFs across architectures, which is a strong data assumption and may limit adoption when such paired data are unavailable.
No inference-time or memory-efficiency comparison is provided, despite the paper motivating weight-space processing as more efficient than rendering-based pipelines.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and emerging problem: performing downstream tasks directly on NeRF weights, especially across heterogeneous NeRF architectures.
The idea of combining graph meta-networks with a contrastive objective to align NeRFs representing the same object under different parameterizations is intuitive and experimentally explored.

The paper includes latent-space analysis, classification, retrieval, and variants with unseen architectures, and compares three training objectives (rendering-only, rendering+contrastive, contrastive-only).
Single-architecture classification results show modest gains over prior methods nf2vec and Cardace et al., indicating that a GMN-based encoder can be competitive in that restricted setting.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method largely combines existing components—GMN encoder from Lim et al. (2024), nf2vec decoder, and the SigLIP contrastive loss—without introducing a new architecture, graph-conversion technique, or learning objective tailored to NeRFs.

Overclaims architecture-agnosticism: the paper claims to embed 'any' NeRF and handle 'arbitrary' architectures, but experiments only cover MLP and tri-plane NeRFs plus synthetic hyperparameter variants. No hash-grid, voxel, or other common NeRF architectures are tested, and graph construction for arbitrary NeRF architectures is not demonstrated.

The contrastive loss requires paired NeRFs of the same object under different architectures during training, which is a strong data requirement and limits practical applicability. It also fails to generalize fully to some unseen variants (e.g., TRI-8C with contrastive-only training reaches only 11.4%).

Evaluation lacks a meaningful multi-architecture baseline: prior methods cannot be evaluated in that setting, but rendering-based baselines or alternative graph-based meta-networks are not explored. Single-architecture improvements over nf2vec/Cardace et al. are marginal (e.g., 93.6 vs. 92.1 and 94.0 vs. 93.1).

The main architecture-agnostic claims are not strongly supported by results: in multi-architecture classification with a classifier trained on BOTH, the proposed contrastive variant L_R+C (91.9%) underperforms the rendering-only variant L_R (93.5%). Cross-architecture classification remains weak (e.g., MLP-trained classifier tested on TRI is 71.9–73.6%), and instance-level retrieval Recall@1 is only 29.0% for BOTH/BOTH and 45.5% for MLP/TRI.

No ablation studies on key hyperparameters such as the contrastive loss weight λ, the choice of contrastive objective, graph construction details, or encoder capacity. Claims about why SigLIP is preferable are not empirically justified against alternatives like InfoNCE.

Unseen-architecture experiments mostly vary hyperparameters within the same two families (MLP and tri-plane). Results for truly different variants are often near chance in some settings, undermining the claim of robust generalization to unseen architectures.

The paper's tables and captions appear inconsistent or malformed in places (e.g., Table 1/3 column headers and caption descriptions do not align cleanly), making the reported results difficult to verify.
Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, and the training setup (2 weeks on a single RTX 3090 for some variants) makes independent verification costly.
The authors acknowledge that the considered NeRF architectures are not state-of-the-art, which weakens the practical significance and impact of the contribution.

strengths: First framework to process NeRF weights across multiple architectures and to generalize to unseen NeRF architectures at inference time, using Graph Meta-Network parameter graphs.

Combines a rendering loss with a SigLIP contrastive objective to encourage an architecture-agnostic latent space; the t-SNE analysis and ablation over L_R, L_R+C, and L_C support the central intuition.

Demonstrates strong classification results in the multi-architecture setting and improved cross-architecture generalization; in the single-architecture setting it matches or exceeds nf2vec and Cardace et al.
Provides a rendering-free inference pipeline for downstream tasks on NeRFs by directly embedding weights, with no need to render views at test time.
Reproducibility details are generally good: architectures, losses, training hyperparameters, hardware, and base codebases are specified.
weaknesses: The 'Any NeRF' claim is overstated: experiments cover only MLP-based and tri-plane NeRFs and a few architectural variants, not arbitrary NeRFs such as hash-grid or other state-of-the-art architectures, nor real-world scenes.
Instance-level retrieval performance is weak overall: the best Recall@1 is around 45.5%, and the rendering-only L_R model achieves 0.0 Recall@1 on BOTH, which undermines claims of robust retrieval.

The multi-architecture setting has no external baselines because prior methods cannot be trained on both architectures; a naive render-then-image-model baseline is missing, making it hard to calibrate the practical benefit of weight-space processing.
Some unseen architecture results show severe performance drops (e.g., L_C on TRI-8C reaches 11.4%, L_R on TRI-16W reaches 30.1%), so robustness is architecture-dependent and not fully established.

The contrastive loss requires paired NeRFs of the same object under different architectures during training, which is a strong data requirement and limits applicability in realistic settings where such paired multi-architecture data may not exist.

The technical novelty is mainly an integration of existing components (GMN encoder, nf2vec decoder, SigLIP loss); the paper does not introduce a new meta-network or NeRF-processing mechanism beyond the contrastive alignment recipe.

strengths: Addresses a clear and relevant problem: architecture-agnostic processing of NeRF weights, enabling downstream tasks without rendering.
First framework to jointly handle MLP-, tri-plane-, and hash-table-based NeRFs, including a novel parameter-graph conversion for multi-resolution hash tables.
Combines a rendering loss with a SigLIP contrastive loss and provides latent-space analysis showing complementary effects on class separability vs. architecture invariance.
Experiments cover 13 architectures from three NeRF families and evaluate both seen and unseen architecture variants.

Achieves strong classification accuracy on seen architectures and competitive or improved results over nf2vec/Cardace et al. in single-architecture settings; first downstream results on hash-table NeRFs.
Provides implementation details, hyperparameters, and qualitative generalization results on Objaverse.
weaknesses: Retrieval results are quantitatively weak: recall@1 ranges from 0.0% to ~33%, and recall@10 is often below 50%, which does not strongly support the claim of effective architecture-agnostic instance retrieval; qualitative examples often show only class-level similarity.

The multi-architecture setting lacks external baselines because prior methods cannot handle diverse architectures; comparisons there are limited to internal loss ablations, and single-architecture improvements over prior work are modest.
Robustness to unseen architectures is uneven, with severe drops for variants such as TRI-8C, TRI-16W, and HASH-11T, which weakens the paper's broad robustness claims.

The proposed hash-table parameter graph omits explicit spatial/hashing information and only connects entries to feature dimensions; this may lose important spatial assignment information, and no ablation compares it with alternative graph constructions.

The contrastive training requires multiple architectures representing each object, a strong data requirement that limits practical applicability and is not addressed for unpaired or single-architecture NeRF collections.
Evaluation is mostly limited to synthetic ShapeNetRender objects, with only a qualitative Objaverse experiment; there is no large-scale, scene-level, or cross-dataset quantitative validation.

The method largely combines existing components (Graph Meta-Network, nf2vec decoder, SigLIP loss), and novelty is mostly in application/adaptation; sensitivity analyses for the loss weighting and graph-design choices are limited.
No code or trained model release is mentioned, so reproducibility may be limited despite the appendix details.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and challenging problem: processing NeRF weights across heterogeneous architectures without rendering, which could enable downstream tasks on NeRF representations.
It proposes a parameter-graph conversion for multi-resolution hash tables, extending prior graph meta-network formulations to a new NeRF family.
The experimental study covers 13 architectures across MLP, tri-plane, and hash-table families, including unseen architecture variations, and provides classification and retrieval evaluations.
The analysis of rendering versus contrastive losses via t-SNE and downstream results gives some insight into architecture-invariance versus class-separation trade-offs.
The method achieves competitive or better single-architecture classification results against nf2vec and Cardace et al. on MLP and tri-plane datasets.
weaknesses: The core novelty is largely incremental: it combines existing components—a Graph Meta-Network encoder, the nf2vec decoder, and the SigLIP contrastive loss—and applies them to NeRFs, with the main technical addition being a hash-table graph conversion.

The evaluation is narrow and insufficient for the broad claims. Training is only on ShapenetRender, a small synthetic object dataset; no large-scale or real-scene NeRF datasets are used for training, and Objaverse is only used for qualitative retrieval.

Retrieval performance is very weak overall. For instance-level retrieval, R@10 on ALL/ALL is only 27.2% with the best loss, and R@1 is 5.3%; this hardly supports the claim of robust architecture-agnostic NeRF retrieval.

The paper overstates architecture-agnostic behavior. t-SNE shows hash-table sub-clusters remain even with the contrastive loss, and the framework still requires manually designed graph conversions per architecture, so it is not fully architecture-agnostic or able to handle arbitrary unseen architectures automatically.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete. nf2vec and Cardace et al. cannot be trained in the multi-architecture setting, and there is no baseline for the hash-table family; many table entries are missing, making the claimed superiority difficult to verify.

The unseen-architecture results contain clear failures, e.g. HASH-11T remains near random accuracy (about 25–29%) and TRI-16W is highly inconsistent across losses, yet these are not sufficiently discussed as limitations of the method.
The contrastive objective is not fully ablated: the choice of lambda is heuristic, no sensitivity analysis is provided, and there are no error bars or multiple-seed evaluations for the main tables.

The paper lacks sufficient evidence for the central claim that the latent space reflects NeRF content rather than parameterization. Classification can still rely on architecture-specific cues, and retrieval results suggest that instance-level invariance is not well learned.

The work does not convincingly establish significance for the broader AI community. It is an application/extension of meta-networks to NeRF weight processing, with limited downstream task scope (classification and retrieval on synthetic objects) and no strong theoretical or empirical advance.

strengths: Introduces the first architecture-agnostic framework for processing NeRF weights, handling MLP, tri-plane, and multi-resolution hash-table architectures within a unified Graph Meta-Network encoder.
Proposes a novel and memory-efficient parameter-graph conversion for multi-resolution hash tables, enabling GMN processing of hash-based NeRFs for the first time.

Combines rendering and SigLIP contrastive losses; the t-SNE analysis convincingly shows that the contrastive objective aligns same-object embeddings across architectures while the rendering loss helps preserve class separability.
Provides a broad empirical study across 13 NeRF architectures from three families, covering single-architecture, multi-architecture, and unseen-architecture settings for classification and retrieval.
Achieves state-of-the-art results in single-architecture classification against nf2vec and Cardace et al. where direct comparison is possible.
The paper is clearly written, with detailed appendices describing graph conversions, training hyperparameters, and qualitative results that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation is mostly limited to ShapenetRender, with only a qualitative Objaverse transfer experiment; generalization to real-world, large-scale, or more diverse NeRF datasets is not quantitatively established.

The claimed 'unseen architectures' are hyperparameter variations within the three architecture families seen at training time; no entirely new architecture family is tested, which weakens the architecture-agnostic generalization claim.

In the multi-architecture setting there are no external baselines because prior methods cannot operate there, so the comparison is only between loss variants; the paper does not compare against rendering-based downstream pipelines.

Instance-level retrieval performance is low in absolute terms, e.g., ALL/ALL recall@10 is 27.2%, which raises questions about practical usefulness despite clear improvements over the rendering-loss-only variant.

Some unseen architecture variations, such as TRI-16W and HASH-11T, remain very challenging with near-chance accuracy, which is in tension with broad claims of robust performance on unseen architectures.

Ablations are limited to loss variants; there is little analysis of sensitivity to the contrastive loss weight, graph representation design choices, or GMN encoder architecture, and code release is not mentioned.

The contrastive training procedure requires paired NeRFs of the same object under multiple architectures, which may limit scalability to existing NeRF datasets where such paired multi-architecture data is unavailable.
